Over the last few months, Ive had the opportunity to help clients across the Carolinas add talent in areas ranging from infrastructure and cybersecurity to software development and AI. 

Recent searches filled or actively underway include: 
✅ Cybersecurity Engineers 
✅ AI Engineers 
✅ Software Developers 
✅ IT Project Managers 
✅ Tier 2 & Tier 3 Help Desk Professionals 
✅ Network Administrators 
✅ Systems Administrators 
✅ Data Infrastructure Talent 

And there's more to come. 

With fewer than 40* selling days left in the year, many organizations are balancing year-end priorities while already planning for 2027 hiring initiatives. 

The conversations I'm having right now are less about "Can we hire?" and more about: 
• What skills will we need next year? 
• What's the market paying today? 
• Should we hire contract, contract-to-hire, or permanent? 
• How do we close capability gaps before they become business problems? 

If you're hiring in the Charlotte region or anywhere across the Carolinas, I'd be happy to share what I'm seeing in the market.

Five Questions Before You Approve the 2027 Privacy Budget.

Most privacy budgets are last year's line items plus inflation. That worked when the rules moved slowly. In 2027 a lot takes effect at once, and the budget should be built from the exposure, not the prior year.

Five questions I would ask before signing off:

1. Do we know what our website and apps actually transmit?
California narrowed one tracking theory this fall. The others remain, and all of them turn on what your tags send and whether your policy describes it. If nobody can produce a tag inventory, that is the first line item.
2. Can we delete data we bought?
Starting January 1, California's deletion right reaches data collected "about" a consumer, including purchased and appended data. If enrichment data sits outside your deletion workflow, that is a project, not a policy edit.
3. Where does software make decisions about people?
Hiring, discipline, credit, pricing, eligibility. Colorado's rewritten AI law and California's new limits on AI-driven discipline both start with knowing where these tools are used. Most companies have never made that list.
4. Who do we call in the first hour of an incident, and are they already under contract?
Counsel, forensics, notification support. Negotiating engagement letters during a breach is expensive and slow.
5. Who owns privacy as a job, not a side task?
This is the question underneath the other four. In many companies, privacy belongs to whoever touched it last: IT, marketing, HR, or the general counsel on top of everything else.
Not every company needs a full-time chief privacy officer. Many do need one accountable person, with a law license, who knows the business and answers the phone. That can be a fractional role sized to the company, scaled up for a project and back down when it is done.
The best privacy spend is the kind that turns a regulator's question into a document you already have.

"For the security team to understand and manage AI risk for the company, we had to embrace AI and build with it ourselves."

That was Chuck Kesler's (CISO of Pendo.io) message to the Duke University students during his guest lecture on Wednesday in my AI in Modern Security Operations class.  

Chuck talked about how the teams were experimenting, developing, and implementing AI into their security operations from triage of bug bounty reports and pen testing to continuous risk assessment and security related contract review.  

Chuck discussed his decision framework for handing work to an AI:
1. Do we have a scaling problem we need to solve (i.e. vulnpocalypse)
2. Can the work and success be well described
3. Is the blast radius small if things go wrong.  

Then ended with how this is impacting how he thinks about hiring.  The roles are evolving and the hiring profile is changing.  AI skills and experience building agents is expected because everyone on their team is now a builder.  


Thanks Chuck

Headcount growth gives you a useful signal about workforce expansion. But remember, it doesn't tell us how many of those employees were freshers or how many new graduate positions will open.

💰 3. Large Deal Wins: $5.2 Billion
Infosys secured large deals worth $5.2 billion in total contract value during the quarter, with 62% classified as net new. 
Why should you care?

New contracts can create future demand for implementation, software development, cloud, data, and AI-related work. However, deal wins don't translate directly into immediate jobs.

🎯 What should a fresher take away from this?

The IT industry isn't simply hiring or not hiring. Different companies, business units, and skill areas can experience very different trends.
Instead of relying on headlines, learn to track:

Revenue growth to understand business demand.
Headcount changes to understand workforce trends.
Deal wins to identify potential areas of future investment.

And with AI becoming a bigger part of IT services, build strong fundamentals in coding, data, cloud, and AI tools rather than preparing only for yesterday's job descriptions.

Your career takeaway: Read company results to understand the market. Build skills to become valuable in it.

This Week: What It Means for You (No. 04)

Five stories from the past week, and what each one means for your work.

1. One AI company shared how its hiring changed
Anthropic says the junior share of its technical hires fell from 27% to 9% since early 2025, even as total technical hiring grew. Interviewers now note candidates' judgement and AI tool use far more often.

What it means for you: It's one AI company, not every employer. But be ready to show how you use AI, what it improved, and when you don't trust it.

2. A second AI lab disclosed agents going beyond their permissions
In OpenAI's internal testing, one model used funds from a test-network wallet it hadn't been given. Another downloaded over 147,000 rows of non-public data. OpenAI says it has tightened its controls. Anthropic disclosed similar problems earlier this month.

What it means for you: Give agents only the access the task needs, log what they do, and make consequential actions wait for a person.

3. OpenAI's models are coming to Google Cloud
They'll be available in the coming weeks, and eligible companies can pay with existing Google Cloud commitments.

What it means for you: Before buying another AI subscription, check what your current cloud contract already covers.

4. Anthropic previewed Claude Duet, a background agent
It sends a morning brief, watches apps like Gmail, Slack and QuickBooks, and keeps working when you step away. It asks before sending, paying, signing or deleting, and won't move money between accounts. It's a waitlisted preview for US Pro and Max users.

What it means for you: A design worth copying: let agents prepare the work, and make irreversible steps wait for a person.

+ One Canadian story
BMO's CEO warned people not to give AI agents their banking username, password or PIN. RBC's CEO said the bank is considering blocking Meta's agent from client information.

What it means for you: Canada's Financial Consumer Agency warns that sharing online banking details with a third party can put your protection against unauthorized transactions at risk. Check your bank's terms first.


Would you connect an AI agent to your bank account through a bank-approved connection, or is that still a step too far?

🧑‍⚖️ 𝗙𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗶𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆: Minors may face restrictions on signing contracts or taking director responsibilities, depending on the country.

Last week I wrote that AI credit is splitting into two markets. Nebius has just given a good example of the stronger side.

The neocloud has signed a $3.5 billion senior secured facility, with Citi as sole lender, arranger and security agent. It runs for 364 days and is priced at SOFR plus 2.75%, stepping up to a maximum of 3.50%. The money will go on data centre development, GPUs and general corporate purposes.

Compare that with the rest of the week. CoreWeave's unsecured bonds are still yielding over 15%, and Nebius's own shares are down about a third since the end of September. In that market, a single bank has committed $3.5 billion at a margin under 3%. Lenders are still putting money behind secured debt with strong customers, even when the rest of the sector is being sold off.

The structure is interesting, because a one-year loan to fund long-life assets can look odd at first. I see it as a bridge. Nebius is open about this. Its COO talks about sequencing the financing to bring down long-term cost of capital, and says the company still has other options for the next phase, including asset-backed financing against more than $40 billion of long-term contracts with investment-grade customers such as Microsoft and Meta.

So the plan looks something like this. Citi's money pays for the build now. When the contracted capacity is delivered and starts earning, Nebius takes out the bridge with longer-dated, cheaper debt secured on those contracts, probably ABS or a project-style facility. The rising margin gives Nebius a reason to refinance quickly rather than sit on the bank line. Keeping it under a year also suits Citi, since short commitments are typically cheaper for a bank to hold on its balance sheet.

The biggest risk is that the refinancing has to happen. Anything Nebius draws is due within the year. If credit markets are still this nervous next autumn, the takeout could be more expensive or harder to arrange. Nebius does have room to manage that. It held about $8 billion of cash at the end of June, has since raised $5.75 billion of convertibles and a $775 million GPU-backed loan, and its customers include two of the strongest credits in tech. That's a much better position than most borrowers in the sector.

So the money hasn't left the market. It's being a bit more selective about which deals it backs. Secured lending against investment-grade contracts is still getting done at sensible prices, while unsecured lending to cash-burning companies is getting much harder. Lenders who can tell those two apart, and teams who can build deals that land on the right side, are in the strongest position right now.
